title: Psalm 50: God Summons His People to Court
summary: God appears from Zion in fire and storm and summons heaven and earth as witnesses while he judges his own people. To the faithful he says he does not need their sacrifices, since every animal already belongs to him; what he wants is thanksgiving, kept vows, and prayer in the day of trouble. To the wicked who recite his covenant while living in theft, adultery, and slander, he warns that his silence was not approval, and that judgment is coming.
story: Psalm 50 interrupts the flow of Book II. It is the only psalm of Asaph in this book (the other Asaph psalms are 73 to 83), and it stands between the Korahite psalms (42 to 49) and the long run of David's psalms that begins with Psalm 51. Its placement seems deliberate: Psalm 50 says God wants a thankful heart more than animal sacrifice, and Psalm 51 follows with David's confession that God desires a broken and contrite heart. Together they present the heart of true worship. The psalm also stands in the line of the prophets, who repeatedly warned Israel that religious ritual without justice and faithfulness was worthless.
historical:
The heading reads “A Psalm of Asaph.” According to Chronicles, Asaph was a Levite singer whom David appointed to lead music before the ark (1 Chronicles 16:4-7), and his descendants continued as a guild of temple musicians after the exile (Ezra 2:41). A psalm “of Asaph” may have been composed by Asaph himself or, more likely in many cases, by or for that guild over a longer period.

The psalm's setting has been debated. Its summons to those “who made a covenant with Me by sacrifice” (verse 5) has led many scholars to propose a covenant renewal ceremony, in which Israel gathered to reaffirm its commitment to God and to hear the law read, as in Deuteronomy 31:10-13 or Joshua 24. Its themes also closely resemble the eighth-century prophets (Isaiah 1, Hosea 6:6, Amos 5:21-24, Micah 6:6-8), so some date it to that era; others think it predates and influenced them. The text does not settle the question.
cultural:
Israel's worship centered on sacrifice. Burnt offerings were wholly consumed on the altar; the thank offering (todah) was a type of peace offering in which part of the animal was burned, and the worshiper and his family ate the rest in a joyful meal celebrating God's help (Leviticus 7:11-15). Vows were promises, often made in times of danger, to offer something to God when he answered prayer.

In the surrounding cultures, sacrifices were often understood as food for the gods, who were thought to depend on human offerings. Mesopotamian texts describe gods who needed to be fed. Psalm 50 mocks that idea: if God were hungry, he wouldn't tell anyone, since the whole world is his. The legal setting is also important: in the ancient Near East, covenants and treaties called on heaven and earth as witnesses, and the prophets used this courtroom language when God brought charges against Israel. Scholars call this form a covenant lawsuit.
literary: The psalm is a divine speech set in a courtroom. Verses 1 to 6 are the summons: God appears in fire and storm (a theophany, or visible appearance of God, recalling Sinai), calls witnesses, and gathers his people. Verses 7 to 15 address the faithful who sacrifice but misunderstand what God wants. Verses 16 to 21 address the wicked who talk about the covenant and break it. Verses 22 and 23 give the verdict and a closing promise. The thank offering appears in both verse 14 and verse 23, framing the psalm's positive message. Most of the psalm is in God's own voice, which is unusual.

outline.t: God appears and summons heaven and earth
To the faithful: I do not need your sacrifices
To the wicked: you recite my covenant but break it
The verdict and the way of thanksgiving

doctrines.note: God is self-sufficient: “the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof.” He needs nothing from us. Worship is therefore not supplying God's lack but responding to his goodness.
God judges his own people first. His silence is not approval (verse 21), and those who speak his words while breaking them stand under his rebuke.
“Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you” sets thanksgiving and petition at the heart of the relationship God wants. Dependence, not ritual performance, honors him.

words.note: Todah, thanksgiving or thank offering. It can mean either the sacrifice or the words of praise that went with it, and the psalm plays on both. God asks for the offering that confesses what he has done, and in verse 23 says it is this that honors him.

Berit, covenant. The faithful made a covenant with God by sacrifice (verse 5), while the wicked carry the covenant on their lips but hate God's instruction (verse 16). The psalm exposes the gap between reciting the covenant and keeping it.

Chasid, faithful one or saint, someone who belongs to God and shows loyal love (chesed) in return. God gathers his chasidim in verse 5 as the people bound to him by covenant, even as he corrects their worship.

christ: Hebrews 13:15 urges believers to continually offer through Jesus a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess his name, language close to this psalm's call for a thank offering. The New Testament presents Christ as the final sacrifice who ends the need for animal offerings (Hebrews 10:1-10), so that thanksgiving becomes the natural worship of those he has redeemed. Jesus also echoes the psalm's critique of religion without righteousness when he rebukes those who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from him (Mark 7:6, quoting Isaiah 29:13). The connection is thematic: the psalm clears away a false idea of worship, and Christ fulfills the true one.

hard.q: If God did not want sacrifices, why did he command them in the law?
hard.a: The psalm does not reject sacrifice; God says plainly in verse 8 that he is not rebuking Israel for their sacrifices. What he rejects is the idea that he needs them, and the practice of offering them while ignoring his commands. The prophets make similar statements that sound absolute (Hosea 6:6, Amos 5:21-24) but are best read as sharp contrasts: God wants mercy more than sacrifice, not sacrifice without mercy. Some scholars read these texts as more radical criticism of the sacrificial system, but most see them as calling worship back to its purpose. Sacrifice was a gift of God to Israel, a way of drawing near, never a service God required for his own sake.

questions: God says, “If I were hungry, I would not tell you.” How might we treat God as though he needed something from us?
The wicked in this psalm recite God's words while living against them. Where is the gap widest between what you say about God and how you live?
What would it look like to make thanksgiving, not duty, the center of your worship?
